headline: Built by an SRE who couldn't unsee it
text:
Digital Safety Knights started with a simple, uncomfortable realization: the same platforms our kids play on every day were built with almost no visibility into what actually happens in their chat systems.

As someone who spent years making sure production systems were observable, reliable, and safe — the lack of basic visibility into children's online spaces was the thing I couldn't unsee.

DSK exists to close that gap: free education for kids, honest information for parents, and eventually, tools that give families the visibility they deserve.

Shield up. 🛡️

headline: Financial sextortion is the fastest-growing threat to teen boys
text:
Most parents picture online predators as a slow grooming process. Financial sextortion breaks that model entirely.

It's fast: an account posing as a teenage girl contacts a teen boy, escalates within hours, then demands payment under threat of exposure. NCMEC's CyberTipline logs thousands of these reports every year — one of the fastest-growing categories they track.

The single most protective step: tell your kids now, before it's needed — "If anyone ever threatens you over a photo, come to me immediately. You won't be in trouble."

Full breakdown (with what to do if it's already happening) in our Monthly Journal: digitalsafetyknights.org

headline: The Roblox chat your child sees isn't the whole picture
text:
Roblox's visible chat filter blocks profanity and obvious keywords. It does not cover private in-experience chat channels, coded language, or the Discord servers that almost every popular Roblox game funnels kids toward.

Parents who review official chat logs and see nothing alarming are often looking in the wrong place.

The fix isn't panic, it's specificity: ask your child to show you which games they actually play, sit with them for 10 minutes, and know whether a Discord server is attached to that game.

We wrote a full breakdown for parents — link in comments.

headline: AI chatbots are the new grooming surface
text:
A single bad actor can now run what amounts to an industrial-scale grooming operation using freely available AI tools — custom personas on roleplay platforms, designed to appeal to kids, available 24/7, at zero marginal cost.

This isn't a hypothetical. It's already documented across multiple platforms.

The practical takeaway for families: roleplay AI platforms (Character.AI and similar) have no appropriate place in a child's digital life, full stop. Not because AI is inherently dangerous — because these specific products are designed for open-ended relationship-building with no safety rails for minors.

More at digitalsafetyknights.org

headline: You cannot out-discipline an engagement algorithm
text:
Infinite scroll, autoplay, and variable-ratio recommendation are the same behavioral mechanics behind slot machines — not by accident, by design.

Screen time limits address quantity. They don't address what a feed is optimizing for during that time. A child can hit a 2-hour limit having spent the whole time in a harmful content spiral.

What actually helps: turning off autoplay, actively curating who they follow, and asking "how does your feed make you feel lately" instead of "how much time did you spend."

The question opens a door that screen-time reports never do.

headline: Omegle shut down. The risk didn't.
text:
In late 2023, Omegle — the random video-chat site synonymous with stranger-danger online — shut down under the weight of child-exploitation lawsuits. Many parents exhaled.

The function it offered didn't disappear. It moved — into successor apps marketing themselves explicitly as "the new Omegle," and into livestream features already built into apps families consider familiar.

The rule we teach kids: if a stranger on any live video asks personal questions, end it and tell a parent immediately. No exceptions, no explaining first.

Full piece in our Monthly Journal.

headline: A 30-minute back-to-school ritual worth keeping
text:
New school year, new devices, new class group chats. It's the best moment all year to reset your family's digital safety setup together.

Our recommended 30 minutes: privacy settings audit, platform-specific protections (Roblox restrictions, private accounts), a written family media agreement, and refreshing your family code word against voice-clone scams.

The families who handle a real incident well aren't the ones with the strictest rules — they're the ones who did this boring setup work months before anything went wrong.

Free checklist at digitalsafetyknights.org

headline: Building this through MITdesignX Le Rosey
text:
Grateful to be developing Digital Safety Knights' product roadmap through the MITdesignX Le Rosey accelerator this year — quests and badges for kids, a free "Glitch Detector" tool teaching red-flag recognition, and eventually Guardian, our on-device monitoring tool built around consent rather than surveillance.

One rule guides every decision: the free safety core for kids is never paywalled. Revenue comes from parents, schools, and grants — never from a child's safety.

More on where we're headed: digitalsafetyknights.org

headline: One password rule that actually sticks with kids
text:
"Passwords are secrets — even from your best friend." Not because friends are untrustworthy, but because friendships change and passwords, once shared, effectively belong to whoever has them.

The same logic extends to a family code word: a word only your household knows, used to verify identity if anyone calls or messages claiming to be a relative in an emergency. Voice-cloning scams targeting families are common enough that this five-minute setup belongs in every family's routine.

Teach the rule once. Refresh the code word every school year.

headline: Deepfakes don't need to be real to cause real harm
text:
Using only a few public photos, image-generation tools can fabricate convincing images used in sextortion attacks — the threat of exposure alone is often enough to coerce compliance, whether or not the image is authentic.

The protective conversation isn't about scaring kids off technology. It's specific: explain that AI can create convincing fake images, that a threat based on a fake image is still a real crime, and that reporting it immediately — never paying, never staying silent — is always the right move.

Resources: NCMEC's CyberTipline and Take It Down tool, linked at digitalsafetyknights.org

headline: What we wish every school counselor knew
text:
Free tier stays free for every school, always — worksheets, curriculum PDFs, and classroom-mode quests with no login required for students.

What we hear consistently from educators: the gap isn't awareness, it's specificity. Generic "be safe online" messaging doesn't compete with the specificity of an actual scam script. Kids need to recognize patterns, not just categories.

If you're an educator or counselor and want a pilot for your school this year, we'd love to talk.

headline: The Knight Council: kids teaching kids
text:
One of the ideas we're most excited about: a teen ambassador program, led by our youth co-founder, where students bring digital safety education into their own schools — with parental consent, moderated, student-led.

Adults explaining online risk to kids will always have a credibility gap. Peers explaining it to peers don't.

If a school-age safety message is going to land, it's more likely to land from someone who was scrolling the same feed last week.

headline: A free 5-minute check most families skip
text:
Our Family Safety Audit walks parents through a short, honest assessment of where the real gaps are — not a generic checklist, a specific one, mapped to the actual platforms kids use today.

No account required, nothing stored, no fear tactics. Just a clear picture of what to fix first.

Try it free: digitalsafetyknights.org/audit.html

headline: The red flags are more consistent than people think
text:
Urgency ("only 10 seconds left"). Secrecy ("don't tell your parents"). Personal questions from strangers. Requests that feel too easy or too generous.

These four patterns show up across almost every scam and grooming attempt we've documented — free Robux offers, fake friend requests, AI chatbots, sextortion openers. Different platforms, same structure.

Teaching a child to recognize the pattern generalizes. Teaching them to avoid one specific scam doesn't.

That's the whole premise behind our free Glitch Detector tool, launching soon.

headline: Why we're looking at Finland next
text:
Finland's reputation in educational innovation makes it a natural first international pilot for DSK's school program — and a credible signal for the partners and funders who ask "has this worked anywhere outside the US."

We're using an upcoming trip to pitch Finnish schools and educators directly. If you have a connection to Finnish education, child safety policy, or ed-tech innovation circles, we'd genuinely welcome an introduction.

The mission travels better with local partners who already have the community's trust.
